content_voiceover: This slide summarizes the mutation spectrum in hemophilia A and B, broken out by severity, and it's the molecular basis for a classic genotype-phenotype correlation. In severe hemophilia A, panel A, the intron twenty-two inversion is the single most common mutation, at about thirty-five percent, followed by missense and frameshift mutations at around seventeen percent each. In mild-to-moderate hemophilia A, panel B, missense mutations alone account for almost eighty percent of cases. The same pattern holds for hemophilia B. Severe disease, panel C, is a mix of missense, nonsense, and structural mutations, while mild-to-moderate hemophilia B, panel D, is overwhelmingly missense, at about eighty-seven percent. The rule to remember is that severe disease is driven by null mutations, ones that produce no functional protein, while milder disease is driven by missense mutations that preserve some residual factor activity. This also explains why null mutations carry a higher risk of inhibitor development, the immune system has simply never seen a functional protein before.
keypoints: Severe hemophilia A is dominated by the intron 22 inversion, about 35% of cases
Missense mutations account for nearly 80 to 87% of mild-to-moderate hemophilia A and B
Null mutations, inversions, nonsense, and frameshift changes, cause severe disease with no functional protein
Null mutations carry higher inhibitor risk than missense mutations
keypoint_voiceover: The pattern to lock in is that null mutations, like inversions, nonsense, and frameshift changes, cause severe disease and carry higher inhibitor risk, while missense mutations, which allow some residual protein function, predominate in mild-to-moderate disease. This genotype-phenotype link is one of the most testable concepts in hemophilia genetics.
